newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - British Gas sees more charges.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - British Gas sees more charges.

text.p: British Gas said more provisions for take-or-pay contracts in its results are inevitable once renegotiations with gas producers are concluded.
His comments come after exceptional charges of a total 304 million stg hit the utility's third quarter outcome.

Finance director Philip Hampton told Reuters that British Gas expects to conclude renegotiations with some gas producers soon. "We should be able to achieve something in the relatively near term," he said.
"(But) when we conclude the renegotiations of the North Sea contracts, inevitably there will be a charge," he added.
On a historical cost basis, British Gas' net loss after exceptional charges widened to 364 million stg after a 181 million loss in the same period last year.

The bulk of the charges, 294 million stg, relate to expected losses stemming from contracts to supply gas to continental Europe. Hampton said British Gas agreed these deals to dampen the losses resulting from the take-or-pay deals with North Sea gas producers.
The take-or-pay contracts oblige British Gas to buy more gas than it wants at fixed levels which are considerably higher than spot market prices.
British Gas said it made more sense to sell some of the surplus gas to the continent -- even below cost price -- than store it in Britain where it would not yield any money at all.
"It is better to make a loss in signing these contracts (to supply the continent) than face the bigger loss of accumulating a large surplus of gas that cannot be sold," Hampton said.

He declined to elaborate on recent speculation that oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group had at some stage considered taking over British Gas. "We have nothing to say about potential takeovers. We are still on track to achieve the demerger by the originally announced timetable," he said.
British Gas plans to demerge into separate trading and transport firms some time in the spring of 1997. The company booked 10 million stg in exceptional charges for the planned break-up.

British Gas said it benefited from increased demand in the third quarter following colder weather than a year ago, but it added low spot gas prices continued to hurt its performance in the competitive market for big industrial users.
This business suffered losses of about 90 million stg compared with 70 million stg in 1995's third quarter, British Gas said.

In the domestic market some 80,000 out of a total 500,000 customers switched to competitors after a pilot project to introduce competition started in the south west of England in April. The domestic market is scheduled to be opened up nationwide in 1998. Overall trading losses widened marginally in the third quarter to 286 million stg from 285 million.
"Our third quarter results are always dominated by the summer when people don't consume much, so the trading performance is never particularly interesting in the that period," Hampton said.
British Gas' transport arm TransCo posted an operating profit of 88 million stg after a three million loss a year ago.

An additional 80 million stg will be spent this year to adress the problems with a new gas billing and service systems, British Gas said after it faced a barrage of customer complaints earlier in the year.
